To ensure that complex concepts are interpreted in a universally comprehensible manner, it is recommended to translate the content into a target language and then back-translate it into the original language. 2. Questionnaires, whether electronic or paper-based, should be reviewed for logical consistency, validity of response options, and appropriate skip patterns. 3. Artificial errors should be introduced during pretesting to assess quality control by measuring the proportion of these errors identified. 4. Electronic questionnaires should be pretested, and necessary improvements and corrections should be made based on the findings. 5. It is essential to verify that the questions are clear to survey participants, understood as intended, and answerable. 6. The test data generated using these instruments should be thoroughly examined to ensure accuracy and reliability. 7. When developing questionnaires, it is critical to consider the target population and local context to ensure the appropriateness of the questions and biomarkers being measured. 8. Biomarkers should be selected based on the specific needs of the population and the objectives of the survey, such as measuring syphilis prevalence among men who have sex with men (MSM) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) rates among people who inject drugs (PWID). 9. The cost of tests, local capacity for conducting them, and the feasibility and legality of exporting samples for external testing should also be considered. 10. Investigators should consult laboratory experts, national authorities, and organizations like the CDC and WHO to ensure the use of up-to-date biomarker assays, specimen handling protocols, and standard operating procedures (SOPs). 11. Quality assurance in laboratory testing involves establishing SOPs for every step of the process, from specimen handling to instrument performance validation. 12. Administrative requirements, such as mandatory record-keeping, data evaluation, and internal audits, should be defined to monitor adherence to SOPs. 13. Corrective actions must be specified for addressing identified problems, with clear documentation and assignment of responsibilities. 14. High-quality employee performance should be sustained through training and adherence to established protocols. 15. Ethical considerations are paramount in survey implementation. Participants must be informed about the specimens being collected, the tests to be performed, the risks and benefits of testing, and how and when results will be returned. 16. Informed consent must also be obtained for storing specimens for future testing, specifying the duration and purpose of storage. 17. Protocols for identifying bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs) must include plans for providing treatment or referrals to appropriate health facilities. 18. Rapid testing is ideal for ensuring that participants receive their results promptly, minimizing the risk of losing contact with participants. 19. For tests requiring off-site analysis, unique codes or identifiers should be used to return results to participants, along with post-test counseling. 20. Investigators are encouraged to use national diagnostic standards rather than algorithms designed solely for surveillance purposes to ensure accurate and actionable results. 21. Collaboration with laboratory experts during the survey design phase is essential to determine local capacity for testing and storage, as well as the selection of appropriate testing platforms and assays. 22. Investigators should consider the availability of resources, including budget, laboratory infrastructure, and human capacity, when selecting biomarkers for inclusion in the survey. 23. Specimen collection, handling, transportation, and storage may incur significant costs, which should be accounted for in the survey planning process. 24. Surveys that collect both biological and behavioral data can provide valuable insights into risk levels and inform public health actions. 25. Investigators should ensure that the data collected contributes to local knowledge and that the country or program has the capacity to act on the findings. 26. It is generally considered unethical to obtain consent for unspecified future testing if investigators already know the tests they plan to conduct at the time of consent. 27. Providing test results to participants is a critical component of survey implementation. Results that could affect clinical care should be returned to participants, along with appropriate counseling and referrals. 28. For specimens tested off-site, results should be returned to participants using secure methods, such as unique codes, and accompanied by post-test counseling. 29. Investigators should ensure that participants have access to follow-up care and treatment, either through direct provision or referral to appropriate facilities.
